patient.chief_complaint: New confusion, left visual field loss, and left-sided weakness found during acute rehabilitation assessment
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Kessler is a 67-year-old right-handed man with a history of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma (status post neoadjuvant chemotherapy and en bloc esophagectomy three weeks ago), atrial fibrillation (anticoagulation discontinued perioperatively and not restarted), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, who was transferred emergently from the acute rehabilitation unit after nursing staff noted new neurological deficits during a routine morning assessment. The patient had been admitted to the rehabilitation facility two days ago following a prolonged postoperative hospital course complicated by a brief episode of aspiration pneumonia that has since resolved. On the morning of transfer, the rehabilitation nurse noticed the patient was having difficulty navigating the left side of his breakfast tray and repeatedly bumped into the doorframe on his left side when attempting to walk to the bathroom. When questioned, the patient seemed confused and was slow to respond, though he had been alert and conversant the evening prior. The overnight nursing notes documented that the patient slept through the night without any reported events, and the last documented neurological check at 22:00 the night before was unremarkable. His wife, who was visiting in the morning, confirmed that he had been at his postoperative baseline the previous evening, engaging in conversation and watching television without difficulty. She noted that when she arrived at 07:30 this morning, he appeared confused, was not tracking objects to his left, and had difficulty using his left hand to hold his coffee cup. There was no report of headache, seizure activity, nausea, vomiting, or fever. Given his history of esophageal cancer, the rehabilitation team was concerned about possible brain metastasis versus a new stroke, particularly in light of his discontinued anticoagulation, and activated a stroke alert for emergent transfer to the emergency department. He arrived in the ED at 08:45. His last known well time is established at approximately 22:00 the night before, roughly 10.5 hours prior to symptom recognition.

results.title: Stroke and Cancer: A Review of Risk, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management
results.authors: Dearborn JL, Urrutia VC, Zeiler SR
results.key_finding: Cancer patients have increased stroke risk through multiple mechanisms including hypercoagulability, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, and tumor embolism. Standard stroke treatments apply but cancer-specific considerations are necessary.

results.title: Perioperative Stroke and the Role of Atrial Fibrillation
results.authors: Mashour GA, Shanks AM, Kheterpal S
results.key_finding: Perioperative stroke risk is highest in the first 2 weeks postoperatively. Patients with atrial fibrillation whose anticoagulation is interrupted have significantly elevated risk.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase recommended within 4.5 hours of onset. For wake-up strokes or unknown onset, DWI-FLAIR mismatch may be used to identify patients who may benefit from thrombolysis.

output.summary: Cancer patients face elevated stroke risk, particularly in the perioperative period when anticoagulation is interrupted and hypercoagulability is heightened. In the acute stroke setting, standard reperfusion treatments apply; recent major surgery within 14 days is a relative contraindication to IV thrombolysis. Cancer-associated thromboembolism may involve both arterial and venous systems, and Trousseau syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis and arterial thromboembolism) should be considered when multiple embolic events occur in the context of active malignancy. Secondary prevention in cancer patients with AF typically involves anticoagulation; DOAC is generally preferred unless cancer-specific factors (e.g., GI malignancy with high bleeding risk) favor LMWH.

Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Reassess timing of anticoagulation resumption post-esophagectomy — bleeding vs cardioembolic risk balance
If LVO present, consider mechanical thrombectomy (surgery recency is not an absolute contraindication)

contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not perform TEE in immediate post-esophagectomy patients without surgical consultation
Do not delay anticoagulation indefinitely once acute stroke risk window passes — recurrence risk is high

key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
Large vessel occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Perioperative period with AF off anticoagulation has very high stroke risk
Reinitiating anticoagulation post-major surgery requires individualized bleeding risk assessment
PCA territory infarct presents with visual field loss and may be underrecognized in delirious/postoperative patients
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
